text: FINSAFETYBENCH: Evaluating LLM Safety in Real-World Financial Scenarios Yutao Hou1*, Yihan Jiang1* , Yuhan Xie1, Jian Yang2, Liwen Zhang1 Hailiang Huang1†, Guanhua Chen3† , Yun Chen1,4† 1Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, 2Beihang University 3Southern University of Science and Technology 4MoE Key Laboratory of Interdisciplinary Research of Computation and Economics Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increas- ingly applied in financial scenarios. However, they may produce harmful outputs, including facilitating illegal activities or unethical be- havior, posing serious compliance risks. To systematically evaluate LLM safety in finance, we propose FINSAFETYBENCH, a bilingual (English-Chinese) red-teaming benchmark de- signed to test an LLM’s refusal of requests that violate financial compliance. Grounded in real-world financial crime cases and ethics standards, the benchmark comprises 14 subcat- egories spanning financial crimes and ethical violations. Through extensive experiments on general-purpose and finance-specialized LLMs under three representative attack settings, we identify critical vulnerabilities that allow adver- sarial prompts to bypass compliance safeguards. Further analysis reveals stronger susceptibility in Chinese contexts and highlights the limita- tions of prompt-level defenses against sophisti- cated or implicit manipulation strategies. Warning: This paper contains prompts from illegal or unethical financial scenarios that may be offensive. 1 Introduction Recent large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in understanding and generating financial text (Nie et al., 2024b; Ding et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Zhang and Yang, 2023). These capabilities make LLMs promising tools for a wide range of financial applications, including invest- ment decision-making (Yang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025; Kundu et al., 2025), financial reasoning (Zhu et al., 2025b; Srivastava et al., 2024; Khatuya et al., 2025), and market analysis (Chen et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024). While these advances create significant opportunities, regulators and policymak- ers have raised concerns about potential misuse. * Equal contribution. †Corresponding Authors. In particular, LLMs could be exploited to conceal accounting fraud, manipulate financial reports, or fabricate transactions, which poses risks to mar- ket integrity and financial stability. This misuse, compounded by the models’ inherent susceptibil- ity to misinformation and adversarial manipula- tion (Yang et al., 2025a), not only violates legal and ethical standards but also damages investor trust. Therefore, systematically evaluating the safety of LLMs in finance is an urgent research priority. These limitations hinder the identification of fine- grained compliance risks and impede rigorous eval- uation of LLM safety in financial settings. With FINSAFETYBENCH, we evaluate main- stream open-source models against three represen- tative jailbreak attacks. We find that some attack variants achieve notably high success rates, and the models demonstrate greater vulnerability when evaluated on Chinese data. Further experiments re- veal that common prompt-level defenses have cer- tain limitations against complex or implicit adver- sarial strategies, which underscores the inadequacy of current LLMs in financial safety scenarios. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose FINSAFETYBENCH, a bilingual red- teaming benchmark grounded in real-world cases to facilitate rigorous safety evaluation in the fi- nancial domain. • We define a fine-grained taxonomy of financial misuse, covering 11 types of financial crimes and 3 categories of ethical violations, filling the gap in finance-specific safety alignment. • Through comprehensive jailbreak and defense experiments, we show that LLMs are vulnerable in financial scenarios and that existing prompt- engineering defenses have certain limitations against sophisticated attacks.1 2 Related Work 2.1 Financial Benchmark Existing financial benchmarks predominantly as- sess knowledge-based question answering (Shah et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024) and reasoning (Chen et al., 2021, 2022; Yoash et al., 2025), and evolving toward higher complexity (Chen et al., 2024a; Xie et al., 2024a; Hou et al., 2024), broader coverage (Jiang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), and comprehensive metrics (Lu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025). In re- sponse, comprehensive safety evaluation frame- works have emerged, supported by general-purpose benchmarks. For example, JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024) evaluates the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks, and SORRY-Bench (Xie et al., 2024b) evaluates safety, including linguistic and prompt-formatting factors. Similarly, Chinese- context benchmarks such as FLAMES (Huang et al., 2024), SuperCLUE-Safety (Xu et al., 2023), and jailBench (Liu et al., 2025) target com- prehensive safety assessments. However, fine- grained evaluations tailored to the highly regulated, security-critical financial domain are still scarce. Recently, TRIDENT (Hui et al., 2025) introduced a financial safety benchmark grounded in the CFA Institute Code of Ethics. Although principled, its heavy dependence on specific Code provisions lim- its case diversity and fails to capture real-world variations. In contrast, FINSAFETYBENCH derives from documented real-world cases; each entry con- stitutes a complete scenario, resulting in broader coverage and more realistic simulations. 3 FINSAFETYBENCH Construction 3.1 Overview An overview of FINSAFETYBENCH is shown in Figure 1. We collect real-world financial miscon- duct cases, including legal judgments and CFA ethics materials, filtered and rephrased by LLMs into harmful instructions. The dataset comprises 1,201 proprietary cases and 680 samples from external sources (TRIDENT (Hui et al., 2025), HarmfulQA (Bhardwaj and Poria, 2023), and HEx- PHI (Qi et al., 2024)), yielding 1,881 bilingually aligned instances. Below, we present a breakdown of the categories and data construction pipeline. 3.2 Problem Categories To enable comprehensive evaluation, we define a two-level taxonomy comprising severe financial crimes and financial ethical violations that remain essential for safety despite their lower severity. Fig- ure 2 illustrates the hierarchical structure of these categories. The detailed definitions of all categories are provided in Appendix C. Financial Crimes This category encompasses illegal activities within the financial industry that inflict serious societal harm, often cause major fi- nancial losses, and may result in criminal prose- cution. These activities constitute critical threats that LLM safety alignment must address.

The resulting collection constitutes the final benchmark, where each data entry comprises the harmful instruction, category, language label, and source tag. 3.3.3 Quality Control To ensure the reliability of FINSAFETYBENCH, we invite graduate students in finance to execute a rig- orous multi-stage verification protocol, as detailed in Appendix M. First, regarding source integrity, they validate each real-world judicial case and CFA mock exam question to guarantee accuracy. Sub- sequently, they manually review the intermediate summarizations generated by Qwen3-32B to miti- gate potential hallucinations or biases introduced by the LLM. Finally, for the red-team instructions rephrased by DeepSeek-V3 and items integrated from public datasets, these students conduct a thor- ough validation to ensure that both Chinese and English versions are consistently harmful and cor- rectly categorized. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experiment Setup Evaluation Models We evaluate six target models on FINSAFETYBENCH, comprising five general-domain LLMs and one finance-specific model. The general models are LLaMA- 3 (AI@Meta, 2024) (Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct), InternLM3 (Cai et al., 2024) (InternLM3-8B- Instruct), GLM-4 (GLM et al., 2024) (GLM-4-9B- 0414), Mistral (Mistral AI Team, 2025) (Mistral- Small-24B-Instruct-2501), and Qwen2.5 (Qwen et al., 2025) (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct), and one finance-specific model: XuanYuan (Zhang and Yang, 2023) (XuanYuan-13B-Chat). These models range in size from 8B to 32B and cover general and finance-specialized variants. This allows us to analyze how model scale and domain expertise affect robustness against jailbreak attacks in the financial domain. We additionally evaluate their baseline performance under original non-jailbroken prompts, finding that general-purpose models main- tain near-zero baseline ASRs, while XuanYuan ex- hibits higher inherent vulnerability (detailed in Ap- pendix G). Comprehen- sive results are provided in Appendix F. Model-wise results We observe substantial vari- ance in robustness, indicating that vulnerability is not solely dependent on model scale. Mis- tral proves the most vulnerable with average ASRs exceeding 90% in both languages, followed closely by Qwen2.5. Conversely, LLaMA-3 and XuanYuan yield significantly lower ASRs, with LLaMA-3 recording the lowest overall figure, likely stemming from the rigorous safety alignment integrated throughout its training stages (AI@Meta, 2024). Similarly, XuanYuan exhibits superior ro- bustness compared to general-purpose models, im- plying potential benefits from its financial-domain tuning. These findings suggest that robustness stems primarily from explicit safety alignment and domain grounding rather than model scale. To val- idate this, we conducted a controlled intra-family comparison between Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and its 72B variant (Appendix H). The 72B model shows no safety improvement and is even slightly more vulnerable, confirming that scaling parame- ters alone do not mitigate financial safety risks. Attack-wise effectiveness Our analysis high- lights distinct performance patterns across different attack methods. Iterative approaches, such as PAIR and ReNeLLM, achieve high ASRs. They progres- sively refine inputs to bypass safeguards, maintain- ing high effectiveness despite their computational costs. Conversely, FlipAttack shows extreme insta- bility. Its ASR reaches 93.3% against Mistral but drops sharply to 6.5% against XuanYuan. This dis- crepancy likely stems from XuanYuan’s tendency to prioritize the explicit character-flipping instruc- tion, effectively overlooking the underlying mali- cious intent. Overall, these results indicate that iterative refinement strategies offer the most robust and consistent jailbreaking capabilities. Language-wise results As illustrated in Fig- ure 3, model vulnerability exhibits significant cross- lingual variation. Despite the semantic equivalence of our bilingually aligned instructions, we observe distinct susceptibility patterns: GLM-4, XuanYuan, and LLaMA-3 yield higher ASRs on Chinese finan- cial crimes tasks. Conversely, Mistral, Qwen2.5 and InternLM3 are more vulnerable to English prompts. These disparities suggest that current safety mechanisms exhibit inconsistent alignment across languages. This inconsistency likely arises from imbalanced training data distributions or in- trinsic language-specific biases within the models. Consequently, our findings underscore the essential need for comprehensive multilingual evaluations to assess LLM safety. 5 Further Analysis 5.1 Evaluation on Closed-Source Models To establish practical relevance, we extend our evaluation to two frontier closed-source models: GPT-5.1 and DeepSeek-V3.2 (685B). We selected these models due to their relatively high initial ASRs. Specific defense prompts are detailed in Appendix D. The results indicate that defenses are significantly more effective on Qwen2.5. PAIR and ReNeLLM generate diverse but semantically equivalent variants through semantic rewriting and word order or style changes, which can undermine detection systems that rely solely on surface patterns or static rules. FlipAttack applies reversible character-level transformations and lever- ages the model’s instruction-following behavior to obfuscate the original intent, effectively masking it as superficial noise. This effectively bypasses defenses based on string matching or keywords. 5.5 Case Studies of Failure Modes in Financial Safety To further examine the security vulnerabilities of LLMs in financial-safety tasks, we analyze the mechanisms by which jailbreak techniques ma- nipulate malicious financial inputs to elicit model responses that should otherwise be refused. We identify several recurrent manipulation strategies, including role reframing, descriptive substitution of explicitly illegal terms, endorsement by authori- tative institutions or experts, induced urgency, fic- tional scenarios, and strategy fusion. These strate- gies exploit domain-specific financial terminology and procedural workflows to bypass built-in safe- guards. These techniques reveal systematic weak- nesses in existing safety mechanisms when LLMs are deployed in realistic financial settings. Detailed definitions and representative examples of these failure patterns are presented in Appendix P. 6 Conclusion In this work, we introduce FINSAFETYBENCH, a bilingual red-teaming benchmark for evaluating LLM refusal of financial compliance violations. The benchmark is developed based on real-world financial crime cases and established ethical viola- tion scenarios, encompassing 14 fine-grained cate- gories of financial misconduct. We evaluate both general-purpose and finance-specialized LLMs un- der three representative jailbreak attacks and un- cover critical vulnerabilities. We find that specific attack variants remain consistently effective, with models exhibiting higher susceptibility in Chinese than in English. Furthermore, common prompt- level defenses often fail against complex or im- plicit adversarial strategies. These findings under- score the urgent need for multilingual, fine-grained safety evaluations and more robust, adaptive de- fense mechanisms. D The details of jailbreak and defense We detail three representative black-box jailbreak techniques employed in our study. • Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement (PAIR): PAIR is an automated, prompt-level jail- break method for black-box LLMs that places an attacker model and a target model in an ad- versarial loop. The attacker model generates a batch of candidate jailbreak requests from an initial prompt. Then, using fewer than twenty black-box queries, it combines security-violation signals from the target model’s responses with chain-of-thought scoring to rank, filter, and se- mantically rewrite the prompts. This iterative process continues until it produces a highly ef- fective prompt capable of bypassing the target model’s safety policy. • ReNeLLM: ReNeLLM is a fully automated jail- break framework based on a two-stage paradigm of prompt rewriting and scenario nesting, re- quiring no white-box gradients or external op- timization. It first leverages the LLM itself to perform semantically-equivalent yet morpholog- ically perturbed transformations on the origi- nal harmful prompt—such as paraphrasing, mis- spelling, code-mixing, and injecting noise—and then randomly nests the rewritten prompt into three generic task templates: code completion, table filling, or text continuation. By exploiting the model’s prioritization of task instructions, the true intent is effectively concealed. The entire process is scored in real time by a harmfulness evaluator and iterates for at most 20 rounds, yield- ing stealthy jailbreak prompts with high success rates and cross-model transferability within min- utes. • FlipAttack: FlipAttack is a single-query black- box jailbreak method that leverages the left-to- right reading bias of autoregressive LLMs. It re- quires no external knowledge; it simply flips the characters or word order of the harmful prompt it- self to generate left-side noise, thereby confusing the target model. Then, using chain-of-thought or role-playing prompts, it guides the model to “flip back” and execute the hidden instruction, thus breaching the safety guardrails with an extremely high success rate in a single interaction. N LLM-Based Evaluation and Human Evaluation Consistency Analysis To validate Qwen3-32B as an automated judge, we perform stratified random sampling across jailbreak methods. For each method we sample 100 exam- ples balanced by the automated judge’s labeled outcome (roughly 50 judge-labeled successes and 50 judge-labeled failures). Three annotators with graduate-level finance training independently label each example. Annotators answer two yes/no ques- tions per sample: (1) is the modified query harmful (i.e., requests actionable wrongdoing)? and (2) does the target model’s reply provide harmful/ac- tionable assistance? A sample is considered a true jailbreak success only if both answers are “yes.” Fi- nal human labels are determined by majority vote. Treating the automated judge as a binary classi- fier (“success” vs. “failure”), the agreement sum- mary against human consensus is: accuracy ≈ 93.6%, true positive rate ≈91.5%, and false pos- itive rate ≈4.2%. These figures indicate high agreement between Qwen3-32B and human con- sensus. Notably, the judge shows a conservative bias (higher precision than recall), implying the au- tomated ASR may slightly underestimate the true human ASR. Overall, the validation supports us- ing Qwen3-32B as a practical, scalable judge for large-scale evaluation.
